headline: Sarvam Launches Dictate API for English and 22 Indian Languages at ₹0.50 a Minute
subheadline: The Bengaluru startup's new developer tool pairs its Saaras v4 speech model with a dictation-tuned Sarvam 105B to turn speech into edited text in one call — and claims far fewer corrections than Google's Gemini in its own tests.
body:
• Sarvam AI launched Sarvam Dictate on Monday, November 23, 2026 — an API that turns speech into edited, ready-to-send text in English and 22 Indian languages.
  • It costs ₹0.50 per minute of audio ($0.33 per hour), with speech recognition and transcript editing combined in a single API call.
  • In Sarvam's own tests, Dictate needed 40% fewer character edits than Google's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe on short English dictations, and 47% fewer across Indian languages and Hinglish.
  • For developers: the API is available now, accepts up to 1,000 custom names and terms per request, and handles live dictation plus recordings of up to an hour — details are on Sarvam's launch post.

Sarvam AI has released Sarvam Dictate, a dictation API for developers building voice typing into their apps, covering English and 22 Indian languages. Announced on Monday, the service is built on a simple observation the company makes in its launch post: people do not speak the way they type. They repeat words, restart sentences, correct themselves mid-thought and use names a speech model may never have heard. Dictate is designed to return the text the speaker meant to write, not a literal transcript.

"Sarvam says the product grew out of Kivi, its own dictation app, where users have dictated more than 30 million words."

How it works

Dictate pairs Saaras v4, Sarvam's speech recognition model, with a version of its Sarvam 105B large language model trained specifically for dictation. In a single API call, Saaras v4 transcribes the audio and Sarvam 105B then edits the transcript — removing filler words, false starts and repetitions, and keeping the version of a sentence the speaker settled on. The API returns both the edited text and the raw transcript.

The system is built to handle the way Indian users actually speak, including switching between English and an Indian language mid-sentence. Developers can also choose the output script: each language in its own script with English words in Latin letters, or the whole sentence transliterated into Latin letters. Sarvam says the product grew out of Kivi, its own dictation app, where users have dictated more than 30 million words.

The accuracy claims

Sarvam's headline claim is accuracy. On 2,691 real English dictations of up to a minute from Kivi users, 4.2% of characters needed editing with Dictate, against 7.0% for Google's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe and 5.3% for AssemblyAI Dictation. On 1,370 dictations in 18 Indian languages, Dictate needed edits to 8.8% of characters against Gemini's 15.5%. On Hinglish dictations, the gap was wider: 6.6% against 17.0% for Gemini. These are Sarvam's own benchmark figures, produced with a published judging methodology the company describes in its launch post; they have not been independently verified.

Apps can also send context with each request — up to 1,000 names and technical terms, such as the CRM record on a salesperson's screen, a product list, or the contacts in a chat. A phonetic matcher passes the editing model only the terms that sound like what was said, and Sarvam says the model was trained to apply a listed term only when the whole sentence supports it. On a public benchmark of clips with names and technical terms in seven Indian languages, Dictate wrote a term the speaker never said in 4.7% of clips, against 5.7% for Gemini and 10.6% for ElevenLabs Scribe v2.

What it costs and what it handles

Dictate is priced at ₹0.50 per minute of audio — $0.33 per hour — with recognition and editing included in the one price. It supports live dictation and uploaded recordings of up to an hour, editing long recordings in sections of about 500 words. Sarvam lists chat messages, sales records, forms and meeting minutes among the intended uses, and Inc42 reports potential applications across customer support, telehealth, medical documentation and sales record updates.

A crowded week for Indian voice AI

The launch landed the same day Murf AI released Finch, a streaming speech-to-text model that the company claims ranks first across 11 Indian languages on the Voice of India benchmark, according to Inc42. India's linguistic diversity is the prize both startups are chasing: Inc42 cites a Nasscom projection that the domestic voice AI market will reach $1.8 billion by 2030. Sarvam, for its part, says it will launch more models across vision, speech and edge AI over the next two weeks — and Dictate follows its recent Token Factory platform, which gives enterprises API access to Sarvam's models alongside global open-weight models.
diaspora_angle: For diaspora developers and businesses serving Indian-language users, Dictate offers a single API for dictation across English and 22 Indian languages at ₹0.50 a minute.

key_takeaways: Sarvam launched Dictate API for speech-to-text in 22 Indian languages.
The service costs ₹0.50 per minute of audio.
Dictate requires 40% fewer edits than Google's Gemini 3.5 for English dictations.
It supports live dictation and recordings up to an hour long.
Sarvam aims to tap into India's growing voice AI market projected at $1.8 billion by 2030.
